## Overview

The Hutsuls are an East Slavic ethnic group living in parts of western Ukraine and northern Romania, especially in Bukovyna and Maramureș. Their historical territory, known in Ukrainian as Hutsulshchyna, extends across parts of Halychyna, Bukovyna and Zakarpattia, including the basins of the Prut, Cheremosh and Seret and the upper flows of Suchava, Bystrytsia Nadvirnianska and Tysa. Hutsul settlements and communities are also found around Kolomyia, Kryvorivnia, Vorokhta, Yasinia, Rakhiv and Romanian Marmarosh. According to the 1930 Romanian census, 12,456 Hutsuls lived in Romania within its borders at that time. Their culture is associated with shepherding, forestry, woodworking, metalworking, textiles, ceramics, music and dance.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Lizhnyk* is a Hutsul rug tradition named in descriptions of Hutsul craftsmanship. The sources identify rug weaving as part of Hutsul material culture.

**Kosiv ceramics** are identified as a distinctive Hutsul ceramic tradition. The sources name the tradition.

Pysanka decorating is included among the practices through which Hutsul culture is represented.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name traditional wood-carving designs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources state that colorful and intricate craftsmanship in clothing is an important representation of Hutsul culture.

### Architecture

Hutsul settlements tend to be dispersed across large areas. Permanent residences known as *grazhda* are built at elevations of up to 1,700 meters above sea level and were constructed as fortified locations protected from wild animals and equipped against enemy attacks. Several generations of one family could live in a grazhda. Other Hutsul buildings had a seasonal function and were used to accommodate herdsmen during the pasturing season. Hutsuls are also known for intricate wooden churches, including those in Kryvorivnia, Vorokhta and Yasinia.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Hutsul craftsmanship includes sculpture, architecture, woodworking, metalworking, especially in brass, pottery and the making of household and material objects. The *bartka*, a shepherd’s axe with a small axe head and long handle, is used for chopping wood, as a cane, for fighting and in traditional ceremonies. Bartkas can be intricately decorated with traditional wood-carving designs and passed from generation to generation, especially upon marriage.

## Music & performance

Hutsul music uses several named instruments. The *trembita*, also given as *trâmbiţa*, is a type of alpenhorn. Hutsuls also use multiple varieties of the fife, or *sopilka*, to create folk melodies and rhythms. Other instruments named by the sources are the *duda*, a bagpipe; the *drymba*, a Jew’s harp; and the *tsymbaly*, a hammered dulcimer.

Hutsul songs and dances form part of the cultural practices through which Hutsul identity is represented. Traditional Hutsul sounds and moves were used by the Ukrainian winner of the 2004 Eurovision Song Contest, Ruslana Lyzhychko. A three-day international festival of folk music and art is held every summer in the village of Sheshory in Ukraine. The sources also state that composer Ludmila Anatolievna Yaroshevskaya composed a work for piano based on Hutsul folk music, titled *Fantasy on Hutsul Themes*.

## Dance & theatre

The sources mention Hutsul songs and dances and state that traditional Hutsul sounds and moves were used by Ruslana Lyzhychko.

An amateur Hutsul theatre was organized in 1911 by Hnat Khotkevych, with Les Kurbas later serving as its director.

## Festivals & rituals

Every summer, the village of Sheshory in Ukraine hosts a three-day international festival of folk music and art. The Romanian Hutsuls have a Festival of Hutsuls at the Moldova-Sulița village in Suceava county. The Pysanka museum and the Museum of Hutsul and Pokuttia Folk Art are located in Kolomyia, Ukraine, and present Hutsul-related culture.

The sources also describe traditional ceremonies associated with the *bartka*, which can be used in ceremonial contexts and passed from generation to generation, especially upon marriage.

## Oral tradition & literature

Hutsul culture includes songs and is represented through the work of writers and artists. Writers associated with Hutsul cultural influence include Ivan Franko, Lesya Ukrainka, Mykhailo Kotsiubynsky, Vasyl Stefanyk, Marko Cheremshyna, Mihail Sadoveanu and Stanisław Vincenz. Sergei Parajanov’s 1965 film *Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors*, based on the book by Mykhailo Kotsiubynsky, portrays scenes of traditional Hutsul life.

The sources describe recent efforts in Ukraine to keep the traditional Hutsul dialect alive.

## Language & religion

In Ukraine, Hutsul dialect is classified among the Southwestern Ukrainian dialects. Its closest counterparts are identified as the Pokuttia-Bukovyna, Boiko and Middle Zakarpattian dialects, although these are also sometimes classified as languages or as dialects of Rusyn. Since the annexation of western Ukrainian regions, including Ivano-Frankivsk and Chernivtsi Oblast as well as Transcarpathia, by the Soviet Union, compulsory education has been conducted only in standardized literary Ukrainian. Grassroots efforts have sought to preserve the traditional Hutsul dialect.

Most Hutsuls belong to the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church and the Ukrainian Orthodox Church.
